options.why: The recursive call sits inside a tuple spread, not in tail position, so the lower depth limit applies: 99 levels resolve but 100 fail.
This version is tail-recursive, but 1,000 levels reach the tail-recursion limit and error.
The recursive call is the whole branch, so tail-call evaluation applies and 999 levels fit under the limit.

options.text: None of them, because every recursive conditional type is limited to about 100 levels
options.why: The limit of about 100 applies only to calls that are not in tail position.

explanation: Since TypeScript 4.5, a conditional type whose branch is directly another instantiation of itself (tail position) is evaluated in a loop, up to 1,000 iterations. Verified with tsc 6.0.3: 999 resolves, 1,000 errors. Recursion inside a spread or another type is not tail-recursive and hits the instantiation-depth limit far sooner: in tsc 6.0.3, 99 levels resolve and 100 fail. Accumulator parameters are the standard fix.
reference: TypeScript 4.5 release notes: Tail-Recursion Elimination on Conditional Types

options.text: `A` is `never` and `B` is `'a' | 'b'`, the other way round
options.why: This swaps the two: keyof a union keeps only shared keys, while the distributive version collects all of them.
keyof applied to the union itself returns only the keys every member has.
Distribution applies keyof to each member separately, so A collects both keys.
The distributive version unions the keys of each member; keyof of a union keeps only common keys.

explanation: For a union, `keyof (X | Y)` is the keys present in every member, here none, so `never`. Writing `T extends unknown ? keyof T : never` distributes first: `keyof { a: 1 } | keyof { b: 2 }` = `'a' | 'b'`. `T extends unknown` (or `T extends any`) is the idiom for "apply this to each union member".

stem: Given `type IfStr<T> = T extends string ? 'a' : 'b'`, which three statements are true? (Choose three.)

options.why: any makes a conditional return the union of both branches.
never is the empty union, so the distributive conditional maps no members.
unknown is not assignable to string, and it is not a union, so the false branch is chosen.

options.text: Writing `never extends string ? 1 : 2` directly, outside a generic, gives `never`
options.why: Without a type parameter there is no distribution; never is assignable to string, so it is 1.

options.text: `IfStr<string | number>` is `'a'`, because one member matching is enough
options.why: Each member is evaluated separately, giving `'a' | 'b'`.

explanation: The special cases depend on whether distribution happens. A naked type parameter distributes, so never gives never and unions split. `any` returns both branches. `unknown` is a plain non-union type that fails the check. A literal `never extends string` is not distributive and is simply true, giving 1.

options.why: Parameters are contravariant: a function accepting any string can stand in for one that accepts only 'a', not the reverse.
This is the covariant intuition, but under strictFunctionTypes parameters are compared in the opposite direction.

options.text: Both are `1`, because parameter types are compared bivariantly
options.why: Bivariance applies only to method-syntax members, not function type expressions under strictFunctionTypes.

options.text: Both are `0`, because function types are only assignable when identical
options.why: Assignability is structural; the wider-parameter function is assignable to the narrower one.

explanation: With `strictFunctionTypes`, a function type is assignable to another if each target parameter is assignable to the source parameter. `'a'` is assignable to `string`, so `A` is 1. `string` is not assignable to `'a'`, so `B` is 0. Method syntax (`{ m(x: 'a'): void }`) is still checked bivariantly, so the same comparison written with methods returns 1.
reference: TypeScript 2.6 release notes: Strict function types

options.why: Inference from an overloaded type uses the last signature, not the first.
Conditional types don't combine overloads; they pick one signature.
When inferring from a type with several call signatures, TypeScript uses the last one.

options.text: `never`, because an overloaded function does not match a single signature
options.why: The match succeeds using the last signature; it doesn't fail.

explanation: The handbook notes that inferring from a type with multiple call signatures, such as an overloaded function, uses the last signature, because it is usually the most general catch-all. So `ReturnType<typeof f>` is `number` and `Parameters<typeof f>` is `[x: number]`. To get every overload you need tricks that match several signatures explicitly.

stem:
What numeric literal type is `CountChars<'hello'>`? Type a number.

```ts
type CountChars<S extends string, A extends unknown[] = []> =
  S extends `${infer _}${infer R}` ? CountChars<R, [...A, 1]> : A['length'];
```
explanation: In `${infer _}${infer R}`, the first infer takes exactly one character (an infer followed directly by another infer matches a single character), and R takes the rest. Each step adds one element to the accumulator: h, e, l, l, o, then '' fails the pattern and returns the length, 5. `CountChars<''>` is 0. The accumulator keeps it tail-recursive.

options.text: `readonly` makes methods impossible to call; remove `readonly` from function-typed keys with a `-readonly` modifier
options.why: readonly only stops reassigning the property; calling it is fine. The real problem is losing the call signature.

options.text: Mapped types skip function-typed properties entirely, so `onLoad` is missing; add it back with an intersection
options.why: The key is still there. Its type is replaced by a mapped object, not removed.

options.text: Mapping a function type yields `{}`; guard functions with a conditional that returns them unchanged
options.why: A conditional guard stops the recursion at function types, so they keep their call signatures.

options.text: The recursion never ends on function types, so TypeScript gives up and uses `any`
options.why: tsc resolves the type without hitting a depth limit; it produces `{}`, not any.

explanation: A homomorphic mapped type over a function type keeps only its properties (it has none), so `DeepReadonly<() => void>` is `{}` and `cfg.onLoad()` errors with "This expression is not callable" (verified in tsc 6). Primitives are passed through, but functions are not. The fix: `T extends (...args: any[]) => any ? T : T extends object ? { readonly [K in keyof T]: DeepReadonly<T[K]> } : T`.
